clue.text: Snooker player shortens his equipment to gain power in competition

parts.note: Steve Davis, six-times world snooker champion

indicators.note: shortening the word for his equipment clips its final letter

parts.note: a snooker player's equipment is his cue

explanation.surface: A snooker star trims his cue to hit harder in a tournament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortens' docks the last letter of CUE, leaving CU.
explanation.definitionFit: The Davis Cup is the international men's team tennis tournament, so it is a competition by name.

clue.text: One wearing protective gear in conduit

indicators.note: a person wearing clothing sits inside it, so one letter goes within the gear

parts.note: PPE is personal protective equipment
the Roman numeral one is I

explanation.surface: Someone in protective kit is crawling through a duct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wearing' puts I inside PPE.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipe is a tube that carries water or gas, the plain sense of a conduit.

clue.text: 40% of numerical facts, 50% lies in America?

indicators.note: forty per cent of a ten-letter word keeps only its first four letters

parts.note: statistics are numerical facts

indicators.note: half of the four-letter word lies is kept, here its back half

explanation.surface: A jibe at statistics: lies, damned lies, and percentages in America.
explanation.walkthrough: '40% of' keeps the first four of ten letters; '50%' keeps the back half of LIES. The question mark flags that America is defined by a familiar short name.
explanation.definitionFit: The States is the everyday short name for the United States of America.

clue.text: At Wimbledon bagel order covered by cheese roll

indicators.note: something covered by another thing sits inside it, so these letters go within the cheese

parts.note: Brie is a French soft cheese
in tennis a bagel is a 6-0 set, a love score, so zero gives O
CH is Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A tennis fan orders a bagel at Wimbledon and gets a cheese roll instead.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'bagel' is tennis slang for a set won 6-0, so nil, which gives O; 'covered by' wraps the cheese round it and the order.
explanation.definitionFit: Brioche is a sweet enriched French bread, often baked as a small bun or roll.

clue.text: City hit hard

parts.note: to bat is to hit, as in cricket
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A city has been struck badly, perhaps by a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: BATH is a Roman spa city in Somerset, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Bath is an English cathedral city famous for its Roman baths, so an example of a city.

clue.text: 'I'd stab criminal', admits gangster in dock

indicators.note: admitting someone lets him inside, so the gangster goes within the scrambled letters
criminal suggests something crooked, so these letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: Al Capone, the Chicago gangster, gives AL

explanation.surface: A gangster in the dock confesses to a violent threat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' rearranges the quote plus 'in' into TIDBASIN, and 'admits' takes Capone's name inside. The 'in' seems to belong to the courtroom picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A tidal basin is an enclosed harbour area whose water level rises and falls with the tide, a kind of dock.

clue.text: Note expensive car with gold and red top

parts.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale
RR is Rolls-Royce, a luxury car
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A flashy luxury car, finished in gold with a red roof.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'red top' is a British tabloid newspaper, so called from its red masthead; the Daily Mirror is one.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mirror, Britain's Daily Mirror, is one of the tabloid newspapers known as red tops.

clue.text: Wireless picks up origins of alien transmission — reading it could heat things up

indicators.note: a radio picking up a signal takes it in, so these letters go inside

parts.note: wireless is an old word for a radio

indicators.note: origins are beginnings, so the first letters of the two words

parts.note: reading is one of the three Rs, so R

explanation.surface: A radio receives an alien signal whose message could inflame things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picks up' puts the two initials inside the radio. Reading is R from the three Rs (reading, writing, arithmetic).
explanation.definitionFit: A radiator is a heater that warms a room, so it is something that heats things up.

clue.text: Breaking bail — one's excuse?

indicators.note: breaking something smashes it apart, so these letters are reassembled

parts.note: the Roman numeral one is I

explanation.surface: A suspect who has skipped bail offers an excuse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking' rearranges BAIL into ALIB.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a claim of being elsewhere at the time, offered as an excuse or defence.

clue.text: Recall 20% off cream hat

indicators.note: recall read as re-call, call back, so the word runs backwards
a fifth of a five-letter word is one letter, so the tail letter is dropped and four are kept

parts.note: the cream is the elite, the best

explanation.surface: A shop recalls a cream-coloured hat and discounts it by a fifth.
explanation.walkthrough: '20% off' trims ELITE to ELIT, and 'Recall' (call back) reverses it. Tile is old slang for a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Tile is old British slang for a hat, especially a silk top hat.

clue.text: Overly tense and risky to catch female mythical figure

parts.note: too means overly, excessively
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

indicators.note: catching something holds it inside, so one letter goes within the other word

parts.note: hairy is informal for risky or frightening

explanation.surface: A nervous attempt to catch a woman who may not even exist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to catch' puts F inside HAIRY.
explanation.definitionFit: The tooth fairy is the imaginary being who leaves money for children's lost teeth, a figure of folk myth.

clue.text: Series of notes in small capitals on drinks

parts.note: SC is the printer's abbreviation for small capitals
ales are beers, drinks

explanation.surface: A typographer sets a run of notes in small capitals on a drinks list.
explanation.walkthrough: Small capitals are a typeface of capital letters at lower-case height.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical scale is a fixed run of notes going up or down in pitch.

clue.text: Refrain from taking holiday without other people?

parts.note: leave is time off work, a holiday
alone means with no one else

explanation.surface: Someone declines to go on a holiday by themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refrain from taking' disguises itself as the start of a sentence about holidays; the question mark marks the playful split.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave something alone is to not touch or take it, so to refrain from taking it.

clue.text: European royal family has swamped Britain with revolting food

indicators.note: a thing swamped is engulfed, so one letter sits inside the other word
revolting read as revolving, turning over, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: grub is slang for food

explanation.surface: A European dynasty has smothered Britain with disgusting food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swamped' puts B inside; 'revolting', read as turning over, reverses the food.
explanation.definitionFit: The Habsburgs were the dynasty that ruled Austria and much of Europe for centuries, a royal house.

clue.text: Sailor upset royal court …

indicators.note: upset means turned over, so in a down entry the word reads from the bottom up

parts.note: AB is an able-bodied seaman
R is the abbreviation for royal, as in RN

explanation.surface: A sailor causes offence at the royal court, continuing into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns AB to BA. The ellipsis joins the clue to 17 down as one story.
explanation.definitionFit: The bar is the lawyers' rail in a court, and by extension the court or legal profession itself.

clue.text: Address thus includes mountain time

indicators.note: including something takes it inside, so these letters go within the word for thus

parts.note: so means thus, in that way
a peak is a mountain

explanation.surface: A speaker's address mentions mountain time, as if giving a time zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'includes' puts the mountain and T inside. 'Address' looks like a noun, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To address someone is to speak to them directly.

clue.text: … boat's just capsized!

indicators.note: a capsized boat is upside down, so in a down entry the word reads from the bottom up

parts.note: but means just or only, as in but a moment

explanation.surface: Continuing the story: the sailor's boat has just overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capsized' turns BUT over.
explanation.definitionFit: A tub is a slow, clumsy boat, informally.

clue.text: Hurry to climb into bed that's cleaned

indicators.note: climbing into the bed puts one word inside the other

parts.note: rush means hurry

explanation.surface: Someone rushes to get into a freshly made bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to climb into' puts the hurry inside the bed; 'that's' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Brushed is a past participle meaning swept or scrubbed clean, as teeth or a coat are.

clue.text: Finally, the Times replaces work from rival advocate

indicators.note: replacing swaps one set of letters for another, here the word for work is swapped out

parts.note: an opponent is a rival
op is a musical work, short for opus

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word the

parts.note: times is the multiplication sign, X

explanation.surface: A newspaper replaces an article by a rival writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replaces' puts E and X in place of OP in OPPONENT. 'the Times' looks like the newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: An exponent is someone who champions an idea or practice, a promoter or advocate.

clue.text: On Irish author said to be merry

parts.note: re means on or about, as in a memo

indicators.note: said signals that the author's name is heard, not written

parts.note: James Joyce, the Irish author of Ulysses

explanation.surface: Someone writes about an Irish author who was reportedly jolly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' signals a sound-alike: JOYCE gives the ending JOICE.
explanation.definitionFit: To rejoice is to feel or show great joy, much like being merry.

clue.text: Graduate stands outside canteen over by the French group

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the whole combination reads backwards
standing outside something surrounds it, so the other word goes within

parts.note: BA is a Bachelor of Arts degree
a mess is a military canteen
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A graduate waits outside the canteen with a French group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stands outside' wraps the graduate round the canteen, giving BMESSA; 'over' reverses that to ASSEMB. A mess is a military dining hall.
explanation.definitionFit: To assemble is to gather or group together.

clue.text: Rabble who are rioting, not acting to support society

indicators.note: in a down entry the support goes beneath, so the society letter sits on top
rioting means running wild, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for acting, as in a job title

explanation.surface: A rioting mob, playing no part, propping up society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rioting' rearranges WHO ARE once 'not' drops A, giving HOWER under S.
explanation.definitionFit: Shower is British slang for a contemptible or useless group of people, a rabble.

clue.text: Ape eats second and third banana on top of the forest

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so these letters go within the word for ape

parts.note: to ape is to copy

indicators.note: only the second and third letters of the fruit are kept

explanation.surface: A monkey munches a banana high in the treetops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second and third' keeps two letters of the fruit; 'eats' puts them inside. 'Ape' is the verb, not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The canopy is the uppermost layer of branches and leaves in a forest.

clue.text: Star bit off vegetable

indicators.note: off means taken away, so these letters are removed from the star's word

parts.note: a star is a celebrity

explanation.surface: A famous star took a bite out of a vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' removes B, I, T from CELEBRITY. 'bit' seems to be the past of bite.
explanation.definitionFit: Celery is a stalk vegetable eaten raw or cooked.

clue.text: Work by English rector in charge of sheets?

parts.note: toil is hard work

indicators.note: in puts the clergyman's letter inside the word for charge

parts.note: a toll is a charge for using a road or bridge

explanation.surface: A clergyman's work involves looking after the bedsheets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts R inside TOLL to make TROLL. The question mark flags that the sheets are not bedding but tissue.
explanation.definitionFit: A toilet roll is a roll of perforated tissue sheets.

clue.text: Quaint boiled sweets unwrapped

indicators.note: boiling churns things up, so these letters are mixed into a new order
unwrapped strips the outer letters off, keeping the inside

explanation.surface: Old-fashioned boiled sweets with their wrappers taken off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unwrapped' strips SWEETS to WEET; 'boiled' rearranges that.
explanation.definitionFit: Twee is British for overly quaint, sentimentally cute.

clue.text: Evil king to fall

parts.note: a sin is an evil deed
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: An evil king is destined to be overthrown.
explanation.definitionFit: To sink is to drop or go down, as a ship does.

clue.text: Pensioners back to front in TV programme

indicators.note: back to front moves the final letter round to the start

parts.note: OAPs are old-age pensioners

explanation.surface: Elderly viewers appear in a television show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back to front' moves the S of OAPS to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A soap, short for soap opera, is a long-running serial drama on television.

clue.text: Wise Sanders has blown his top

indicators.note: blowing his top here means losing the topmost letter

parts.note: Bernie Sanders, the US senator

explanation.surface: The usually wise Senator Sanders has lost his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has blown his top' removes the B of BERNIE. Ernie Wise was half of the British comedy double act Morecambe and Wise.
explanation.definitionFit: The comedian Ernie Wise shares his first name with the answer, so Wise is his surname clue.

clue.text: The end of acts in play touring old city

indicators.note: touring means going round, so the scrambled letters surround the city
play means move freely, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: Ur was an ancient city of Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: A play's final act goes on tour to an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'play' rearranges the two words into CTAINS, which 'touring' wraps round the old Mesopotamian city.
explanation.definitionFit: Curtains is informal for the end, the finish of something, from the theatre curtain falling.
